title: Immunology, immunisation and herd immunity
blurb: Explain how vaccines create immunity, protect whole populations, and who is offered what under the UKHSA schedule from September 2026.
question: A woman who is 30 weeks pregnant attends her antenatal appointment in October. She has not had any vaccines in this pregnancy. Which vaccines can the nurse explain she is eligible for today?

teach.body: Immunity is the body's ability to protect itself from infectious disease. Innate immunity is present from birth and is non-specific: intact skin and mucous membranes, gastric acid, phagocytes and complement. Acquired immunity is specific to one organism or a close group. It is gained actively (your own immune system makes it) or passively (you receive ready-made antibodies). In plain English: innate is the castle wall; acquired is a guard trained to recognise one particular enemy.

teach.caption: Active immunity uses B cells (antibodies) and T cells (cell-mediated). Passive immunity is borrowed and temporary.

teach.body: Vaccines induce active immunity and immunological memory. A first dose of an inactivated vaccine or toxoid produces a primary response, mainly IgM at first and then IgG; young infants may need two or more doses (the primary course). Later doses give a faster, larger IgG secondary response. Memory means the body responds rapidly when it later meets the real infection. Inactivated vaccines cannot cause the disease they are designed to prevent.

teach.caption: Plain polysaccharide vaccines (for example PPV23) give poor, shorter protection in infants and young children; conjugation fixes this.

teach.body: The primary aim of vaccination is to protect the person vaccinated. But vaccinated people are also less likely to pass infection on, so people who cannot be vaccinated, such as young babies or some immunosuppressed people, are protected too. This is population or 'herd' immunity. Example: teenagers receive MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which reduces carriage of meningococci in young people and so protects infants. If coverage falls, diseases can return.

items.label: PCV and MenB boosters, MMRV dose 1

teach.caption: Check the SCID newborn screening result before giving rotavirus (and BCG). Children aged 2 to school years: annual nasal flu (LAIV).

head: Who
Offered
rows: Flu any stage; Tdap from 16 wks; RSV from 28 wks
teach.caption: Clinical risk groups (for example diabetes, chronic heart, lung, liver or kidney disease, asplenia, immunosuppression) are offered annual flu and pneumococcal vaccines.

items: Consent is a process, not a one-off signature, and can be withdrawn at any time.
Consent for a whole course need not be sought again for each dose unless new information arises, but it is good practice to check the person is still willing.
Young people of 16 and 17 are presumed capable of consenting.
A Gillick competent child under 16 can consent, and a parent cannot override that consent.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Amina at the antenatal clinic
teach.body: Amina is 30 weeks pregnant in October and has had no vaccines this pregnancy. The practice nurse explains three: inactivated flu (any stage during the flu season), pertussis as Tdap (from 16 weeks, ideally before 32 weeks but still worthwhile later) and RSV (Abrysvo, from 28 weeks). She explains that antibodies cross the placenta to protect the baby in the first weeks of life (passive immunity), answers questions and records consent.
teach.cite: UKHSA Complete routine immunisation schedule, from 1 September 2026

teach.text: Since September 2026 MenB is given at 8 AND 12 weeks and the infant PCV dose moved to 16 weeks. Older charts showing PCV at 12 weeks or MenB at 16 weeks are out of date.

items: Active immunity is made by your own immune system and lasts; passive immunity is borrowed antibody and lasts weeks to months.
Live attenuated: MMR, BCG, yellow fever. Inactivated vaccines cannot cause the disease. Conjugates (Hib, PCV, MenACWY) work in infants.
Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
Infants: 8 weeks 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus; 12 weeks same; 16 weeks 6-in-1 + PCV; 1 year PCV, MenB, MMRV.
Pregnancy: flu any stage, Tdap from 16 weeks, RSV from 28 weeks.

summary: You can now explain innate, active and passive immunity, the main vaccine types and how population immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated. You can also apply the UKHSA schedule from September 2026 to infants, pregnant women, older adults and risk groups, and handle consent for vaccination.

A.q: A mother asks why her 6-week-old baby did not catch measles when an older sibling had it. Which type of immunity best explains this?
options: Active immunity from natural infection
Innate immunity from intact skin
Passive immunity from placental antibodies
Active immunity from a primary vaccine course
A.why: Antibodies transferred across the placenta give passive immunity. It is more effective against some infections, such as measles and tetanus, and lasts a few weeks or months (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.0: The baby has not had measles, so has not made its own antibodies against it.
whyNot.1: Innate barriers are non-specific and would not explain protection against one particular virus.
whyNot.3: A 6-week-old has not yet started the routine schedule, which begins at 8 weeks.

A.q: Which of these vaccines contains a live attenuated organism?
options: Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)
Tetanus and diphtheria toxoid
Pneumococcal polysaccharide (PPV23)
Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR)
A.why: Live attenuated vaccines include MMR, yellow fever and BCG. The weakened organism replicates in the recipient and usually gives a full, long-lasting response after one or two doses (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.1: Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain inactivated toxins (toxoids).
whyNot.2: PPV23 contains capsular polysaccharide, not a living organism.

A.q: A parent asks what vaccines her baby will have at the 16-week appointment under the schedule from 1 September 2026. What is the correct answer?
options: 6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus (oral)
6-in-1 and pneumococcal (PCV)
PCV, MenB and MMRV
6-in-1, MenB and PCV
A.why: From 1 September 2026 the 16-week visit is the third 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) plus PCV (Prevenar 13). MenB is given at 8 and 12 weeks (UKHSA schedule, September 2026).

whyNot.0: 6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus is the 8-week and 12-week visit, not 16 weeks.
whyNot.2: PCV and MenB boosters with the first MMRV dose are given on or after the first birthday.
whyNot.3: MenB is no longer given at 16 weeks under the September 2026 schedule.

B.q: Why are conjugate vaccines such as Hib, PCV and MenACWY used in infants rather than plain polysaccharide vaccines?
options: Joining it to a protein gives immune memory in young children
Conjugate vaccines contain live bacteria that replicate in the infant
Plain polysaccharide vaccines cause the disease in children under 2
Conjugation removes the need for any booster doses later in childhood
B.why: Plain polysaccharides give a poor, short-lived response in infants. Attaching the polysaccharide to a protein carrier (conjugation) lets the immune system respond more broadly and provide immunological memory, even in young children (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.1: Conjugate vaccines are not live; they contain polysaccharide joined to a protein.
whyNot.2: Polysaccharide vaccines are not live and cannot cause the disease; their problem is a weak response.
whyNot.3: Boosters are still part of the schedule, for example PCV and MenB at 1 year.

B.q: Raj, 72, takes no regular medicines and has never had a shingles vaccine. He asks whether he is eligible. What is the most accurate reply?
options: No, shingles vaccine is offered at age 65 and not later
No, as he did not have it when he turned 70
Yes, adults aged 70 to 79 are offered Shingrix
Yes, but he needs to wait until he turns 75
B.why: The September 2026 schedule offers Shingrix to people turning 65 (from 1 September 2023 onwards) and to adults aged 70 to 79, plus severely immunosuppressed people aged 18 and over.

whyNot.0: The 70 to 79 age group is also eligible, as well as those turning 65.
whyNot.1: Eligibility covers the whole 70 to 79 range, not one birthday.
whyNot.3: Age 75 is the routine age for RSV vaccine, not shingles.

B.q: A nurse explains why it matters that school-age children are vaccinated even though a disease is now rare. Which statement best describes population immunity?
options: Vaccinated children cannot catch, carry or pass on the infection to others
Once a disease becomes rare, routine vaccination can safely be stopped
Unvaccinated people receive protective antibodies from their vaccinated contacts
Fewer vaccinated people spread infection, so the unvaccinated are protected
B.why: Vaccinated individuals are less likely to be a source of infection, so people who cannot be vaccinated still benefit. If coverage is not maintained the disease can return (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.0: No vaccine offers 100% protection; some vaccinated people still become infected.
whyNot.1: The Green Book warns diseases can return if high coverage is not maintained.
whyNot.2: Antibodies are not transferred between contacts; that would be passive immunity by placenta or immunoglobulin.

C.q: Jodie, 26, is 22 weeks pregnant and attends in late September. She had the pertussis vaccine in her last pregnancy two years ago. Which vaccines should the nurse offer today?
options: Flu and RSV now, with Tdap after 28 weeks
Flu now, with Tdap and RSV both from 28 weeks
Tdap now, with flu deferred until after the birth
Flu and Tdap now, with RSV from 28 weeks
C.why: Each pregnancy: inactivated flu at any stage in the flu season, Tdap from 16 weeks (ideally before 32 weeks) and RSV (Abrysvo) from 28 weeks. At 22 weeks she can have flu and Tdap now; RSV is offered from 28 weeks (UKHSA schedule, September 2026).

whyNot.0: RSV vaccine is offered from 28 weeks, and Tdap is due from 16 weeks, so this reverses the timing.
whyNot.1: Tdap is offered from 16 weeks, so there is no need to wait for 28 weeks.
whyNot.2: Flu vaccine can be given at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season.

C.q: Mrs Okoye consented to her son's full primary course. At the 12-week visit she says she has read new information online and has questions about one vaccine. What should the nurse do?
options: Proceed, as her consent covered the whole course
Discuss her questions and confirm consent first
Give the doses and answer questions afterwards
Ask her to sign a new form for every vaccine
C.why: Consent is a process and may be withdrawn at any time. Course consent need not be sought again for each dose unless new information has come to light, and it is good practice to check the person is still willing (Green Book chapter 2, 2025). Here she has raised new information.

whyNot.0: Course consent does not apply where the parent raises new concerns; consent must be checked.
whyNot.2: Vaccinating before addressing her concerns means consent may not be valid.
whyNot.3: A new written form for each vaccine is not required; a discussion and confirmation is.

C.q: Tom, 68, has type 2 diabetes and lives with his wife, who is having chemotherapy. Which advice best applies the September 2026 schedule to Tom?
options: Annual flu and pneumococcal vaccines, which also help protect his wife
Annual flu now, with pneumococcal vaccine deferred until he reaches 75
RSV vaccine now, because diabetes qualifies him from the age of 65
Pneumococcal vaccine now, with flu offered to his wife but not to him
C.why: At 68 with diabetes, Tom is offered annual flu (65 and over, and a clinical risk group) and pneumococcal vaccine (routine at 65 and for diabetes). Household members of immunosuppressed people should also be considered for flu vaccine, which helps protect his wife (UKHSA schedule, September 2026).

whyNot.1: Pneumococcal vaccine is routine at 65 and offered to people with diabetes; 75 is the RSV age.
whyNot.2: RSV at 65 to 74 is for chronic respiratory or heart conditions or immunosuppression; diabetes is not listed for RSV.
whyNot.3: Tom is aged 65 or over and has diabetes, so annual flu vaccine is offered to him as well.

reteach.title: Training the guards
reteach.question: Think of the immune system as a castle. How do vaccines train the guards without letting the enemy in?

blocks.h: Show the guards a wanted poster
blocks.body: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or part of the germ: a weakened live germ (MMR), a killed germ (IPV), a disarmed toxin (tetanus toxoid) or a sugar coat glued to a protein (PCV). The body makes antibodies and memory cells. When the real germ arrives, the guards recognise it at once. Babies borrow some antibodies from their mother through the placenta, but these fade within weeks or months.

blocks.h: From first dose to lasting protection

blocks.text: Passive immunity (placenta, immunoglobulin) is quick but temporary. Active immunity (infection or vaccine) takes time but lasts. Vaccines give ACTIVE immunity.

explain.body: Active immunity is produced by your own immune system after infection or vaccination and is usually long-lasting. Passive immunity is protection from antibodies made by someone else, usually across the placenta or from immunoglobulin, and lasts weeks to months.

test.q: A person exposed to hepatitis A is given human normal immunoglobulin. What type of immunity does this provide?
options: Active and long-lasting
Passive and temporary
Innate and non-specific
Cell-mediated and lifelong
test.why: Immunoglobulin provides ready-made antibodies: passive immunity that starts within a few days but may last only a few weeks (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.0: The person's own immune system has not made these antibodies, so it is not active immunity.
whyNot.2: Innate immunity is barriers and phagocytes present from birth, not donated antibody.
whyNot.3: Immunoglobulin is antibody-based and short-lived, not a lifelong T-cell response.

explain.body: Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, BCG, yellow fever) replicate in the body. Inactivated vaccines (IPV) and toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria) cannot cause disease and need a primary course and boosters. Conjugate vaccines (Hib, PCV, MenACWY) attach polysaccharide to a protein so infants respond.

test.q: Which vaccine contains inactivated toxins rather than whole organisms?
options: BCG
Tetanus vaccine
MMR
Yellow fever vaccine
test.why: Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines contain inactivated toxins called toxoids (Green Book chapter 1).

whyNot.0: BCG is a live attenuated vaccine.
whyNot.2: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine.
whyNot.3: Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine.

explain.body: 8 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 12 weeks: 6-in-1, MenB, rotavirus. 16 weeks: 6-in-1 and PCV. On or after the first birthday: PCV, MenB and MMRV. Check the SCID screening result before rotavirus.

test.q: A baby attends for the 12-week immunisations under the schedule from 1 September 2026. Which vaccines are due?
options: 6-in-1, PCV and rotavirus
6-in-1 and PCV
6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus
MenB, PCV and MMRV
test.why: From September 2026 the 12-week visit repeats the 8-week vaccines: 6-in-1, MenB and the second rotavirus dose. PCV is given at 16 weeks (UKHSA schedule).

whyNot.0: PCV moved to 16 weeks; MenB is due at 12 weeks.
whyNot.3: MenB and PCV boosters and the first MMRV dose are given at 1 year.

explain.body: At 65: pneumococcal vaccine and annual flu. Shingles: turning 65 and aged 70 to 79. RSV: at 75, care home residents, and from September 2026 people aged 65 to 74 with chronic heart or respiratory conditions or immunosuppression. From 1 October 2026 people experiencing homelessness aged 16 and over are offered flu and PCV20.

test.q: Brenda, 69, has heart failure and has not had an RSV vaccine. Under the schedule from September 2026, what applies to her?
options: She becomes eligible for RSV vaccine at 75
She is eligible for RSV vaccine at 70
She is eligible for RSV vaccine now
She is eligible if she moves into a care home
test.why: From September 2026 RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) is offered to people aged 65 to 74 with chronic respiratory or heart conditions such as heart failure, or immunosuppression (UKHSA schedule).

whyNot.0: 75 is the routine age, but her heart failure makes her eligible now at 69.
whyNot.1: There is no age-70 threshold for RSV; people aged 65 to 74 with heart failure are eligible now.
whyNot.3: Care home residence is another route, but she already qualifies through heart failure.
